# Identifying Priorities to Improve the System of Care for Children with Complex Health Needs in North Carolina: Process and Outcomes of Systematic Stakeholder Engagement

**Authors:** Sahil Sandhu; David Y. Ming; Carter Crew; Madlyn C. Morreale; Shea Cleveland; Jennifer Lail; Neal A. deJong

## Abstract

Children with complex health needs (CCHN) have both medical (e.g., chronic conditions) and health-related social needs (e.g., potentially adverse social determinants of health) that require ongoing healthcare and support from multiple community service providers. National standards developed for populations defined by health needs (CYSHCN) provide a framework for stakeholders to plan system-level improvements in care delivery for CCHN, but improvement efforts should reflect the priorities of their families and providers. This article describes a process of prioritizing system-level efforts to improve the health and well-being of CCHN and families in North Carolina (NC), using systematic stakeholder engagement and modified Delphi expert ratings.

We surveyed stakeholders with experience caring for CCHN using an open-ended, 3-item instrument to identify opportunities to improve systems of care. Using directed qualitative content analysis, we synthesized responses into a master list of potential improvement topics. Using a modified Delphi approach, a 16-member advisory committee rated all topics for importance and urgency, on 9-point Likert scales over two rounds; then ratings for each topic were ranked (low, medium, high) to establish relative priority.

47 individuals from 31 counties around NC provided survey responses, yielding 59 improvement topics in 10 domains. Through the modified Delphi method process, 21 topics (36%) received the highest rankings, largely representing access to community- and home-based services, equity, and enhancement of the pediatric workforce.

Priorities identified by stakeholders will inform advocacy, policy, and improvement efforts. Next steps for the coalition include developing improvement projects to implement stakeholder-recommended actions for the highest-priority topics.

## BACKGROUND

Children with complex health needs (CCHN) (a) have chronic conditions that require ongoing health care, and (b) face resource challenges (e.g., potentially adverse social determinants of health, inadequate access to services) that complicate management of their health needs. CCHN are defined by intersections among medical and social conditions that affect health,1,2 and require services from multiple medical and non-medical systems.3 Two well-characterized groups comprise CCHN: children and youth with special healthcare needs (CYSHCN)4 and children with medical complexity (CMC).5 Together, these groups account for about 20% of children6, but for a disproportionately high percentage of child healthcare costs and service utilization.7 But not all CYSHCN and CMC have complex health needs; CCHN are those whose social needs complicate management of their conditions, challenge coordinators and providers across the range of service sectors, and make achieving health and well-being elusive (Figure 1).2

Unfortunately, the services CCHN and their families require have traditionally operated in siloes, placing burdens on families to navigate and secure them. For families this responsibility often is stressful and burdensome.8,9 In academic medical centers, providers for the most medically complex CCHN have begun to dedicate personnel and resources to provide intensive support and coordination among members of the care team.10–12 These “complex care” programs improve the quality and experience of health care for many CCHN13, but have at least two notable shortcomings. The first is a limitation of scope: by situating services within health care centers, these programs address fragmentation of medical care but often not its critical intersections with other human services on which families of CCHN rely, such as early childhood care, schools, food assistance, housing support, and child welfare. The second is a limitation of scale: medically-focused complex care models have restricted capacity for enrollment, can be difficult to access for families who live geographically distant from academic centers, and often exclude children whose health needs are primarily due to complex behavioral and social conditions, even though these are relatively more prevalent and have a large impact on population health.14

Child health experts have recognized these shortcomings and developed blueprints for stakeholders to integrate services across sectors. One key example is the “Standards for Systems of Care for CYSHCN,” developed by the Association of Maternal and Child Health Programs in 2014.15 Though focused on all CYSHCN, not explicitly those with concomitant social needs (i.e., CCHN), the standards outline a comprehensive, family-centered system of care, ranging from health insurance to access to care and community-based services. While these standards provide foundational language and goals to inform a national agenda to advance systems of care for CCHN, states must identify and support their own priorities. This is because health-focused interventions are implemented at the state and local levels and should reflect the needs and context of families they serve. North Carolina (NC) is currently positioned to advance the system of care for CCHN, given the state’s multi-payer push towards value-based care,16 the current transition to Medicaid managed care,17 and the launch of the federally-funded North Carolina Integrated Care for Kids (NC InCK) model in five counties.18

Thus, in 2020 we convened a multi-sector group of stakeholders to form the Children’s Complex Care Coalition of North Carolina (4CNC). The mission of 4CNC is to advance an integrated system of care for CCHN in NC. The first goal was to identify priorities for system-level improvement through stakeholder engagement and consensus development. In this paper, we describe and report the outcomes of a multi-step prioritization process that identified topics most important and urgent to key stakeholders to improve the system of care for CCHN in NC.

## METHODS

### Overview

This project’s activities took place between August 2020 and January 2021. According to the Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI) Model for Improvement, the first step of the improvement process is to establish aims (i.e., defining “what are we trying to accomplish?”).19 A bottom-up approach that seeks input from a diverse array of stakeholders can help define system improvement aims that best reflect the needs of patients and their families.20 To identify priorities for improving the system of care for CCHN in NC, we used a multi-step prioritization process that included qualitative analysis of open-ended surveys and a modified Delphi consensus process (Figure 2).21

### The 4CNC Advisory Committee

Created in July 2020, 4CNC is a multi-sector, interdisciplinary coalition of stakeholders across the state with the common goal of improving the health of CCHN.22 The project described was organized by representatives from Duke University, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, and Legal Aid of North Carolina. The 4CNC coalition included 4 founding team leaders, 4 student volunteers, and 16 advisory committee members. The advisory committee represented a diversity of sectors that serve CCHN and individual roles, and included 3 parents of CCHN, 3 state public health officials, 6 pediatricians from diverse practice settings, 1 Medicaid leader, and 3 representatives of child service and advocacy agencies. The coalition was also supported by the National Center for Complex Health and Social Needs, which provided content expertise on complex care systems, and operational support and funding to host a series of regional convenings to operationalize the priority agenda.23

### Step 1: Open-ended Survey to Develop Improvement Topics

The four team leaders and full advisory committee developed an open-ended survey to identify potential system improvement topics. Each member of the advisory committee invited five to six contacts with experience caring for CCHN (two-thirds parents, one-third service providers such as private-duty nurses, habilitative therapy providers, agency coordinators, and primary care providers) from around the state to complete the survey online (Qualtrics©, Provo, UT). Available in both English and Spanish, the survey was designed to elicit suggestions to improve the system of care for CCHN from those with lived experience. Respondents reviewed introductory information about the purpose of the survey, then shared free-text responses to three prompts: (1) “the two most important issues in the system of care that must improve so that children with complex needs in NC can receive the best possible care in their homes and home communities”; (2) “the two most important steps that leaders in NC can take to address the key issues you identified just above”; and (3) “strengths in the system of care in North Carolina we should build on as we work to improve care and health for children with complex needs.” We received responses over an 8-week period between August-October 2020.

### Step 2: Directed Content Analysis and Formation of Master Topic List

The four project leads (SS, DM, CC, Nd) then coded free-text survey responses using directed qualitative content analysis to synthesize topics.24 We developed a codebook a priori using the eight named domains and associated standards of the National Standards for Systems of Care for CYSHCN, while also allowing for new, emergent codes after data collection. We piloted the codebook with a subset of responses to ensure internal consistency in coding across team members, and we revised several codes to reflect mutual understanding of the coders. Each individual, free-text response was then independently coded by two team members in Microsoft Excel©. Discrepancies were resolved via discussion until mutual consensus was reached across the four coders. Using the final set of codes and the associated quotes, we created a master list of suggested topics by reducing similar quotes to neutrally worded statements that incorporated key terms from the National Standards for Systems of Care for CYSHCN. Supplementary Figure 1 presents an example of this process. We repeated this process for all assigned codes until we agreed through consensus that the full range of responses to the open-ended survey had been captured. The resulting master list of improvement topics was presented to advisory committee members to rate during the next stage of the prioritization process.

### Step 3: Delphi Rating Process with Advisory Committee

Members of the advisory committee were invited to participate in an online Delphi rating process. In an electronic survey, members were asked to rate the importance and urgency of each improvement topic. Importance was defined as the following: “The topic describes a significant problem that affects the health and/or wellbeing of children with complex health needs and their families. Not addressing the topic will have negative consequences for their ability to achieve and maintain health in their home communities.” Urgency was defined as the following: “The topic is sufficiently severe, widespread, and/or inadequately addressed that it should receive the highest priority for action now in North Carolina.” Members rated topics separately in each area (i.e., importance and urgency) on a 9-point Likert scale (e.g., 1 = not at all important, 5= somewhat important, 9 = extremely important).

After the first rating round, we grouped mean ratings of topics into three relative-priority ranks (called low, medium and high). We grouped ratings to account for expected skew towards higher scores among the majority of topics and to make feasible the subsequent step in the coalition’s work – participatory discussions with stakeholders around the state to develop recommendations for action on the highest relative-priority topics.21 Cutoffs between groups were determined by plotting histograms of mean ratings, identifying natural gaps between mean scores, and discussing proposed cutoff points with the advisory committee.

These cutoffs were used to create overall levels that considered both importance and urgency:

- Level 1: Topics with “high” mean ratings for both importance and urgency

- Level 2: Topics with “high” mean ratings for one, or “medium” mean ratings for both

- Level 3: Topics with “low” mean ratings for both, or “low” mean ratings in one and “medium” in the other.

After the first round, topics in Level 1 were automatically elevated to the final set of priority topics for system-level improvement. Topics in Level 3 were dropped from consideration for the final priority list. Between the first and second rounds, the four team leaders held a virtual meeting with the advisory committee to clarify understanding of topics, address questions about ratings, and develop consensus on the topic ranking process, including the proposed numeric cutoffs for rating levels 1–3. In the second rating round, the advisory committee re-rated Level 2 topics, which were presented along with the mean ratings for importance and urgency from the first round. After that round, levels for topics were recalculated, and topics that moved from Level 2 to Level 1 were added to the final set of priority topics in the 4CNC agenda for improving the system of care for CCHN in NC.

The coalition subsequently operationalized the agenda of priority topics into a set of recommendations co-created with broad participation of families, policymakers, and service providers through a series of virtual stakeholder conferences held in January – March 2021. Those conferences and their findings are beyond the scope of this paper and described in detail elsewhere,25 but are briefly summarized in the Discussion. This work was deemed exempt from review by the Duke Health Institutional Review Board.

## RESULTS

### Topic Development

Open-ended survey respondents (n=47) varied in area of focus, years of experience in their main role in the system of care (parent and/or front-line provider), ethnicity, and geography (Table 1). Respondents represented nearly a third (31%) of counties across NC, in their residence or work. Nearly two-thirds (64%) of respondents were parents or primary caregivers of CCHN. Over a quarter (26%) were clinical providers, such as physicians, nurses, advance practice providers, social workers, and care coordinators. 11% of respondents self-identified as community agency or social service providers. Since individual 4CNC advisory committee members invited respondents independent of the leadership team, response rates were not calculated due to an unknown denominator.

The survey resulted in 130 individual, free-text responses that were synthesized into a list of 59 priority improvement topics (Supplementary Table 1). The 59 topics represented all 8 core domains of the National Standards for Systems of Care. Since some responses did not fit clearly into any of the existing domains, we created two new domains and sub-topics to represent emerging themes: “health equity” and “lobbying and advocacy.”

### Advisory Committee Topic Ratings

In the first rating round and virtual discussion between rounds, 12 of 16 (75%) of advisory committee members participated. In the second rating round, 8 (50%) members participated. Based on plotted histograms of Round 1 advisory committee mean ratings for importance and urgency, we defined high importance topics with mean ratings greater than 8.0 (on a scale of 1–9); medium importance topics with mean ratings between 7.2 and 8.0; and low importance topics with mean ratings below 7.2. We defined high urgency topics with mean ratings greater than 7.8; medium urgency topics with mean ratings between 7.0 and 7.8; and low urgency topics with mean ratings below 7.0.

After Round 1, 12 topics reached Level 1 (20% of all 59 initial topics), 23 topics Level 2 (41%), and 24 topics Level 3 (39%) (Table 2). Topics in Level 1 were automatically included in the final set of priority improvement topics, and topics in Level 3 were dropped from consideration. After Round 2, nine topics improved from Level 2 to Level 1. After the two rounds, a total of 21 topics (36% of initial topics) across all 10 thematic domains reached Level 1, and thus represented the consensus priority list of improvement topics (Table 3). Topics largely represented access to healthcare-, community- and home-based services, health equity, and enhancement of the pediatric workforce across service sectors.

## DISCUSSION

The aim of this multi-step prioritization process of stakeholder engagement and Delphi ratings was to identify priority topics that were most urgent and important to improve the system of care for CCHN in North Carolina. Findings revealed 21 priority topics across 10 domains. The highest-ranked topics were related to access to physical health, behavioral health, and social services across settings, including at home and in the community.

The resulting health-system improvement topics were diverse in both subject area and in scope. Prioritized topics spanned all eight domains of the National Standards for Systems of Care, demonstrating its relevance and appropriateness for adaptation to the case of CCHN in North Carolina.15 We identified topics in two additional domains, health equity and lobbying and advocacy, which may reflect national changes since the National Standards were published in 2017. Topics also ranged from broad thematic areas, such as eliminating health disparities for children from different backgrounds, to narrow ones, such as Spanish-language translation of online patient-portal materials. The heterogeneity and complexity of topics indicates that the prioritization process successfully engaged and elevated the voices of a wide set of stakeholders, most importantly families and frontline providers across sectors.

To translate priority topics into recommendations, the coalition subsequently hosted a series of virtual statewide convenings in early 2021 to further explore the highest priority topics and identify concrete improvement actions. During the three virtual convenings, 90 participants from across the state (including families of CCHN, direct service providers in health care and other sectors, policymakers, and agency representatives) discussed the 21 highest priority topics in small groups facilitated by members of the 4CNC advisory committee. For each topic, participants were asked to draw from their experience to further characterize current challenges; to crowdsource local best practices; and to identify short- and long-term actions the coalition could take together.25 Following the convening sessions, members of the leadership team and advisory committee have partnered with interested convening participants to begin planning and implementing advocacy, policy, quality improvement, and research efforts.

The list of priority improvement topics aligns well with existing developments to improve integrated care in North Carolina. For example, findings demonstrate the importance of early identification of CCHN and addressing social needs in healthcare settings. In the ongoing transformation to Medicaid managed care in NC, managed care organizations are required to conduct comprehensive assessments26 and screen all children with Medicaid for social needs, such as food, housing, transportation, and interpersonal safety.17 Similarly, the new “tailored plans” for individuals with complex developmental, behavioral, and/or mental health needs in NC Medicaid managed care will help integrate systems for physical and behavioral health. Thus, mapping existing efforts in the state and identifying opportunities for alignment in efforts to advance health for CCHN in NC will be crucial for building on existing momentum efficiently.

At a national level, the results of this prioritization process relate to initiatives to develop complex care ecosystems in other states. Although complex care has become a high priority for payers and policymakers in the shift towards value-based payment models, previous efforts have failed to fully include families with lived experience and stakeholders from non-medical sectors.1 This prioritization process demonstrates how academic medical centers can work with with diverse family and professional partners to develop a shared improvement effort. Similar models include the Oregon Pediatric Improvement Project, which facilitates quality improvement activities and learning collaboratives between public and private partners.27 Furthermore, the complex care field has largely focused on adults,28,29 despite strong evidence of the connection between child well-being and health later in life.30 More research is needed to study the implementation and effectiveness of these cross-sector improvement efforts for improving the health and experiences of CCHN and their families.

This work has limitations that should be acknowledged. Though parents of CCHN on the advisory committee helped develop the open-ended survey prompts, we did not evaluate or revise the prompts through cognitive interviews or field testing. While the open-ended survey participants were diverse in family and professional roles, they only represented about one-third of the 100 counties in the state, and disproportionately represented the Triangle region of the state (Raleigh/Durham/Chapel Hill, NC). Future work should explore if and how priorities vary by geography and settings. Similarly, the findings reflect local state needs and context, and may not be generalizable outside North Carolina. Attrition of advisory committee members over the course of the Delphi process limited sources of stakeholder input, particularly in survey round 2. Inability to participate at that stage (December 2020) was likely due to increased personal and professional burdens from the COVID-19 pandemic, as the members who could not attend all work in and/or lead organizations involved in pandemic response (e.g., school nurse, pediatricians). However, we did have representatives from all included sectors participate in all steps of the prioritization process.

## CONCLUSION

Efforts to improve the system of care for CCHN should reflect the needs and context of families they serve. A prioritization process involving parents and service providers identified topic areas most important and urgent to focus future improvement efforts in practice, policy, and research. Priorities identified by stakeholders will inform ongoing stakeholder engagement, advocacy, policy, and quality improvement initiatives focused on systems of care for CCHN in NC. Stakeholder engagement throughout the life cycle of efforts to improve the system of care for CCHN may enhance the impact of those efforts.
